etymology: From grease, for the hair oil and pomade combed through a slicked-back pompadour, and perhaps also for the motor grease of the garages and filling stations where many of these young men worked. The word had an earlier, ugly use in the nineteenth century as an ethnic insult, which this entry does not repeat. In the 1950s and early 1960s greaser named a working-class youth in a leather jacket, white T-shirt, and rolled jeans — the motorcycle-and-hot-rod crowd that respectable parents worried about.
biblical_def: In 1957 every high school had its greasers: boys with pompadours shining with hair oil, leather jackets, a comb in the back pocket, and engine grease under the fingernails from the after-school job at the filling station. The well-to-do kids looked down on them, and some of them earned it with fistfights and switchblades. But many were simply working boys from working homes, rough in manner and loyal to their friends. Grandpa knew both kinds. Scripture has a word for those who sort people by their hair and their jacket. James warns the church to "have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons" (Jas 2:1), and Proverbs reminds us, "The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all" (Pro 22:2). Our Lord said, "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment" (Joh 7:24). The Lord who chose fishermen and a tax collector did not look first at their clothes; "the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). At the same time, the greaser’s swagger was often pride wearing a leather jacket, and rebellion for its own sake is no virtue. So a Christian grandfather teaches both lessons: do not despise the boy with grease on his hands, and do not admire the boy who makes trouble his style. Christ calls both kinds, the scorned and the scornful, to Himself.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s; from the hair oil and the motor grease) for a working-class youth in leather and slicked-back hair — a word that sorted boys by appearance, though the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
webster_full: GREASER, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) A working-class young man with slicked-back, oiled hair, a leather jacket, and a tough manner; often linked with motorcycles and hot rods. "Mom didn’t want me riding around with the greasers from the filling station."

Webster (1828) — GREASE, noun 1. Animal fat in a soft state; oily or unctuous matter of any kind, as tallow, lard; but particularly the fatty matter of land animals, as distinguished from the oily matter of marine animals.
Decode for families: do not judge the boy by his hair; do not imitate the swagger.
scriptures: Jas 2:1
My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
Pro 22:2
The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all.
Joh 7:24
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
corruption_summary: A label of class and style that invited contempt from one side and swagger from the other; Scripture rebukes both respect of persons and proud rebellion.
corruption_paragraphs: Greaser was often a sneer. Respectable families used it to wall off boys whose fathers worked with their hands, and that contempt is exactly the respect of persons James forbids (Jas 2:1). Many a so-called greaser grew into a faithful husband, a deacon, and the best mechanic in the county.

The other side is honest too. Some young men took up the look as a badge of rebellion, wearing toughness and contempt for the "square" world as a style. Pride and scorn are no better in a leather jacket than in a tailored suit. The gospel humbles the snob and the rebel alike, and seats them at the same table.
roots_summary: Latin crassus (thick, fat) → Old French graisse → English grease → greaser (one who greases) → 1950s slang for the slick-haired, leather-jacketed youth.
roots_lines: Latin crassus — thick, fat
Old French graisse — fat, grease
English grease; greaser, one who greases machinery
19th c.: an ugly ethnic use, now rightly abandoned
1950s: the slick-haired, leather-jacketed working-class youth
usage: "They called him a greaser in high school. He fixed every car in our church for forty years and never charged a widow."
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment (Joh 7:24).
The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all (Pro 22:2).

etymology: American high-school word of the late 1940s and 1950s. Dances were held in school gymnasiums, and students were asked to take off their hard-soled shoes to protect the varnished floor, dancing in their socks — hence sock hop, with hop an older slang word for an informal dance. The records came from a turntable on the stage, and the dance became one of the fixed memories of 1950s teenage life.
biblical_def: A sock hop in 1955 was a Friday night in the gym: crepe-paper streamers, a record player on the stage, a chaperone by the punch bowl, and two hundred pairs of saddle shoes lined up by the door because the coach would not have them scuffing his floor. Girls in full skirts and boys in pressed slacks danced in their socks. For most of them it was clean, happy, and awkward. Scripture does not frown on that kind of joy. There is "a time to mourn, and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4), and when the prodigal came home, his brother "heard musick and dancing" (Luk 15:25). The Psalmist could even say of God, "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing" (Psa 30:11). The shoes by the gym door bring another picture to mind. When Moses came near the burning bush, the Lord said, "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground" (Exo 3:5). A sock hop was not holy ground, but the habit of taking care for the place you stand is a good one. Grandparents can teach the young that joy is a gift, that the dance floor has its proper limits, and that the deepest gladness is the gladness of the Father who runs to meet a returning son. Every lesser celebration points to that one.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American high school, late 1940s–50s) for an informal dance held in the gym with shoes off to save the floor — a picture of the proper "time to dance" (Ecc 3:4) and of joy kept within bounds.
webster_full: SOCK HOP, n. (Silent Generation slang, late 1940s–50s) An informal school dance, usually in a gymnasium, where students danced in their socks to protect the floor. "Are you going to the sock hop after the game Friday?"

Webster (1828) — SOCK, noun [Latin soccus; ] 1. The shoe of the ancient actors of comedy. Hence the word is used for comedy, and opposed to buskin or tragedy. 2. A garment for the foot, like the foot of a stocking.
Decode for families: shoes off for the floor’s sake; joy with limits for the soul’s sake.
scriptures: Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing.
Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;
Exo 3:5
And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
corruption_summary: A wholesome word for clean, chaperoned fun; the only caution is the old one that every dance floor needs boundaries of modesty and purity.
corruption_paragraphs: There is very little to correct in sock hop. Chaperoned school dances with punch and records were among the most innocent amusements of any generation, and Scripture plainly allows for joy and dancing (Ecc 3:4).

The caution is perennial rather than particular. As the music changed later in the decade, some dances grew less modest, and a few young people slipped out to the parking lot. The old wisdom holds: rejoice in the gift, keep the bounds of purity, and let every celebration remain one a grandparent could watch without blushing.
roots_summary: Latin soccus (light shoe) → Old English socc → sock + slang hop (informal dance) → sock hop (late 1940s–50s school gym dance).
roots_lines: Latin soccus — a light, low shoe worn by comic actors
Old English socc — a light slipper; later a short stocking
18th c. slang hop — an informal dance
Late 1940s–50s: sock hop, the shoeless dance in the school gym
usage: "Your grandmother and I met at a sock hop in 1954. I stepped on her toes all night — at least I was in my socks."
Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing (Psa 30:11).
Let them praise his name in the dance (Psa 149:3).

etymology: American slang, shortened from soda jerker, the clerk who worked the soda fountain in a drugstore or confectionery; the name comes from the jerking pull on the fountain’s tap handles. The longer form is older; the short soda jerk was in wide use by the 1920s and 1930s, and the soda jerk, in white jacket and paper cap, was a fixture of American towns through the 1950s, with a lively counter lingo of his own.
biblical_def: In 1950 the soda fountain was the heart of a small town, and the soda jerk was its host: a teenage boy in a white jacket and a paper cap, pulling the tap handles, building banana splits, and calling orders in a lingo all his own. Many a grandfather had that job, and it taught him to smile at strangers, count change honestly, wipe the counter without being told, and keep the line moving on a hot Saturday. It was service work, and Scripture holds service in high honour. Our Lord said of Himself, "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mar 10:45). He took a towel and washed His disciples’ feet, and then said, "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet" (Joh 13:14), ye also ought to serve one another. Even a small act of serving counts with Him: "whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward" (Mat 10:42). So the boy behind the counter, if he served "heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23), was doing kingdom work with a scoop in his hand. Grandchildren who wait tables or bag groceries today stand in the same honourable line. The King of glory knelt to serve; no honest service is beneath us.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1920s–50s; from pulling the fountain taps) for the drugstore soda-fountain clerk — humble service work honoured by the Son of man, who came not to be ministered unto, but to minister (Mar 10:45).
webster_full: SODA JERK, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1920s–50s; short for soda jerker) The clerk who mixes and serves sodas, malts, and sundaes at a soda fountain. "He worked as a soda jerk at the corner drugstore all through high school."
Webster (1828) — JERK, noun A short sudden thrust, push or twitch; a striking against something with a short quick motion; as a jerk of the elbow.
Decode for families: the jerk was the tap handle, not the boy; the job was service, and service is Christlike.
scriptures: For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
corruption_summary: A wholesome job-name with nothing to correct; the jerk in it is the pull on the tap, and the soda jerk himself is a fine example of humble service.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to repent of in soda jerk. The jerk in it is the pull on the fountain tap, not an insult to the boy, and the job itself trained a generation in courtesy, honesty, and hard work behind a counter.

If anything, the word corrects us. A culture that looks down on service work forgets that the Lord of glory took a towel and served (Joh 13:14). A Christian family can tell the story of Grandpa’s fountain job with pride, and teach the grandchildren that no honest work done for others is small in God’s sight (Mat 10:42).
roots_summary: Medieval Latin soda (plant ash) → soda water + jerk (a sudden pull) → soda jerker → soda jerk (1920s–50s) → the drugstore fountain clerk.
roots_lines: Medieval Latin soda — a plant ash used in glassmaking; origin uncertain
19th c.: soda water, carbonated water from the fountain
jerk — a sudden pull; the fountain clerk jerked the tap handles
soda jerker, shortened to soda jerk by the 1920s–30s
1950s: the white jacket, paper cap, and counter lingo of every town drugstore
usage: "Your grandfather was the soda jerk at Miller’s Drugs, and he still makes the best chocolate malt in the family."
For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister (Mar 10:45).
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord (Col 3:23).

etymology: American barbershop word, common by the 1950s, for a crew cut trimmed so that the hair on top stands up and is cut level, like a flat deck. The short military haircut came home with the servicemen of the Second World War and became the clean-cut look of the 1950s. (In wartime Navy talk flattop was also a nickname for an aircraft carrier, a separate use from the same picture.)
biblical_def: In 1955 a flat top was the haircut every mother wanted for her boy: buzzed close on the sides, stood straight up on top with a dab of wax, and leveled so flat you could set a playing card on it. Fathers who had worn crew cuts in the service brought the look home, and on a Saturday morning the barbershop was full of boys getting their flat tops touched up for church. It was a neat, plain, cheap haircut, and there is nothing in it to repent of. Scripture’s interest in hair is gentler than we might think. Our Lord said that God’s care for His children is so detailed that "the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Mat 10:30). Every generation has its haircut; God counts the hairs under all of them. Proverbs gives the young and the old each their own glory: "The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head" (Pro 20:29), and "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31). So the boy with the flat top in 1955 is now the grandfather with the white fringe, and Scripture says the second look is the more glorious, if it crowns a righteous life. What matters is not the cut but the heart under it, for "the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). Christ, who numbers every hair, came to make that heart new.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American barbershop, 1940s–50s; brought home from the service) for the crew cut trimmed level on top — a plain, tidy haircut on heads whose very hairs are all numbered (Mat 10:30).
webster_full: FLAT TOP, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s) A crew cut in which the hair on top is cut short and level so that it stands upright; also written flattop. "Get a flat top before school starts, and use the wax so it stands up."

Webster (1828) — FLAT, adjective [Latin latus, broad; Gr.; Eng. blade.] 1. Having an even surface, without risings or indentures, hills or valleys; as flat land. 2. Horizontal; level; without inclination; as a flat roof; or with a moderate inclination or slope; for we often apply the word to the roof of a house that is not steep, though inclined.
Decode for families: every generation has its haircut; God numbers the hairs under all of them.
scriptures: But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
corruption_summary: A wholesome word for a plain, tidy haircut with nothing to correct; the only caution is the timeless one against judging a boy by his hair, whether short or long.
corruption_paragraphs: Flat top carries no sin. It names a neat, practical haircut that came home with the servicemen and suited a generation that valued order and plainness. A tidy head is no virtue in itself, but neither is it a fault.

The caution is about judging. In the 1950s the flat top was taken as the sign of the good boy and the ducktail as the sign of the troublemaker, and adults often read a boy’s heart from his hair. The Lord does not (1Sa 16:7). A Christian family can enjoy the old haircut stories and still teach that character, not a cut, marks a godly young man.
roots_summary: Old Norse flatr (level) + Old English top (summit) → WWII crew cut → flat top (1940s–50s barbershop) → the clean-cut look of the decade.
roots_lines: Old Norse flatr — level, even
Old English top — summit, crown of the head
WWII: the short military crew cut
1940s–50s barbershop: flat top, the crew cut leveled on top
Navy talk, a separate use: flattop, an aircraft carrier
usage: "Every boy in my Sunday school class had a flat top and a clip-on tie."
But the very hairs of your head are all numbered (Mat 10:30).
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).

etymology: American slang of the 1950s for a hairstyle in which the long sides were combed back with hair oil to meet at the back of the head in a vertical part, resembling a duck’s tail feathers. It was also known by a coarser name, politely abbreviated D.A. The style came with the early rock-and-roll era and was worn by the greaser crowd; school principals and barbers often disapproved of it. Who first cut it is not established with certainty.
biblical_def: If the flat top was the haircut mothers wanted, the ducktail was the haircut they feared. A boy would grow his sides long, slick them with hair oil, and comb them back with great ceremony until they met at the back like a duck’s tail, with a curl falling over the forehead in front. It took a comb, a mirror, and a good deal of time, and it announced that he was not a square. The coarser nickname for it told you what the boys thought of the adults who objected. Grandpa may have worn one. Scripture’s first word is about the time spent at the mirror: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?" (Mat 6:27). Peter warns against adorning that is only "outward adorning of plaiting the hair" (1Pe 3:3), and points instead to "the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:4). Hair is not the trouble; vanity is, and the swagger that sometimes came with the comb: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Pro 16:18). And the crude nickname reminds us of Paul’s rule for the tongue: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth" (Eph 4:29). A grandfather can laugh about his ducktail and still tell the truth: a boy who spends an hour on his hair and no time on his soul has the order backward. Christ makes the heart new, and a new heart puts the comb in its proper place.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s; early rock-and-roll era) for the oiled hairstyle swept back to meet like a duck’s tail — a sign of rebellious style and mirror-time, set against the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4).
webster_full: DUCKTAIL, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) A man’s hairstyle in which the long, oiled sides are combed back to meet at the nape like a duck’s tail; also called by a coarser name abbreviated D.A. "The principal told him to cut that ducktail or not come back Monday."
Decode for families: hair is not the problem; the mirror and the swagger can be.
scriptures: Mat 6:27
Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
corruption_summary: A hairstyle worn partly as a badge of rebellion, with a crude nickname attached; the hair is not sin, but the vanity, swagger, and coarse talk around it can be.
corruption_paragraphs: Long hair combed back with oil is not a sin, and many a decent boy wore a ducktail because his friends did. Adults who judged every ducktailed boy a delinquent were often unjust, and Scripture forbids judging by appearance (Joh 7:24).

Still, the style was chosen partly to defy, and its common nickname was vulgar on purpose. Hours at the mirror can feed vanity, and a defiant look can feed contempt for parents and teachers. Scripture’s remedy is not a barber but a new heart: the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4) and a mouth kept clean of corrupt communication (Eph 4:29).
roots_summary: Old English duce (duck, the diver) + tægel (tail) → ducktail (1950s hairstyle) → D.A. → the rock-and-roll era’s rebel look.
roots_lines: Old English duce — duck, literally "diver"
Old English tægel — tail
1950s: ducktail, oiled sides combed back to a point at the nape
Abbreviated D.A. from a coarser nickname
Worn with the leather jacket of the greaser crowd
usage: "Your grandfather had a ducktail in 1956, and it took him longer to comb it than it took me to get ready for church."
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall (Pro 16:18).
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth (Eph 4:29).

etymology: From Hindi dungri, a coarse, cheap cotton cloth associated with the area of Dongri near Bombay (Mumbai), known to English traders from the seventeenth century. Sailors wore work clothes of the cloth, and the plural dungarees came to mean sturdy work trousers or overalls; the U.S. Navy issued blue dungarees as working uniform. To the Silent Generation, dungarees was the everyday name for blue denim work pants — what their grandchildren call jeans.
biblical_def: When Grandpa was a boy, nobody said jeans; they wore dungarees. They were stiff blue work pants you bought a size too long and rolled up at the cuff, and you wore them to do chores, to fix the car, to work the farm, or to scrub the deck if you were in the Navy. They were not a fashion; they were what you put on to work. Scripture has a good deal to say about clothing, and it begins in mercy. After the fall, "Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them" (Gen 3:21). God Himself was the first maker of work clothes for a fallen world. Our Lord told us not to fret about what we wear: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin" (Mat 6:28). The plain cloth of the working man is no shame in God’s sight; of the virtuous woman it is said, "Strength and honour are her clothing" (Pro 31:25). And the clothing that matters most is not cotton at all: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14). A grandfather in dungarees with grease on his knees, and the righteousness of Christ on his soul, is better dressed than a king in purple without it. The old work pants teach the young that clothes are for use and modesty, and that the soul’s garment is the gift of God.
webster_summary: Silent Generation word (from Hindi dungri, coarse cotton; Navy and farm usage) for sturdy blue work trousers before they were called jeans — plain working clothes, and a reminder to put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 13:14).
webster_full: DUNGAREES, n. pl. (Silent Generation usage, 1940s–50s; from Hindi) Sturdy work trousers or overalls of blue denim or coarse cotton; blue jeans. "Put on your dungarees before you go out to help your father with the car."
Decode for families: Grandpa’s dungarees are your jeans — work clothes that became everyday clothes.
scriptures: Gen 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
Mat 6:28
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
corruption_summary: A plain, wholesome word for work clothes with nothing to correct; it preserves the older view of clothing as useful and modest rather than a statement.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in dungarees. The word belonged to sailors, farmers, and mechanics, and the clothes it named were cheap, sturdy, and modest. They fit a generation that dressed for the job in front of it.

If there is a lesson, it is in the change of names. When dungarees became jeans, work clothes became fashion, and fashion became a way of announcing who we are. Scripture points the other way: clothe the body for use and modesty, and clothe the soul in Christ (Rom 13:14).
roots_summary: Hindi dungri (coarse cotton cloth, linked with Dongri near Bombay) → English dungaree (17th c.) → plural dungarees, work trousers → Navy working uniform → Silent Generation word for blue jeans.
roots_lines: Hindi dungri — coarse, cheap calico, linked with Dongri near Bombay
17th c.: English traders’ dungaree cloth
Plural dungarees — work trousers or overalls of the cloth
U.S. Navy: blue dungarees as working uniform
1940s–50s: everyday word for blue denim pants, later jeans
usage: "We didn’t say jeans. We said dungarees, and you only wore them to do chores."
Strength and honour are her clothing (Pro 31:25).
But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 13:14).

etymology: American name of the 1940s and 1950s for calf-length women’s trousers, originally worn for bicycle riding — cut short so they would not catch in the chain or the pedals, hence the name. In use by the 1940s, they became a casual summer staple of the 1950s, worn with flat shoes and a blouse for picnics, gardening, and errands; the same cut is now usually called capris.
biblical_def: Pedal pushers came into Grandma’s closet in the 1950s: cotton slacks cut off at the calf, first for riding a bicycle without catching the hem in the chain, then for picnics, gardening, and Saturday errands. They were practical and cool in July, and for the time a little daring; some mothers thought a lady ought to wear a skirt to the grocery store. Families still remember the arguments. Scripture does not hand us a pattern book, but it does give principles for dress. The first is modesty: women are to "adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9). The second is that outward things are not the main thing: "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning" (1Pe 3:3), but "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4). The third is freedom from anxiety about clothes, for our Lord said of the lilies, "That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these" (Mat 6:29). A grandmother can tell her granddaughter honestly that styles change every decade, that modesty does not, and that the loveliest clothing God gives is the robe of His Son’s righteousness. Within those bounds a Christian family can choose with a clear conscience, and pedal pushers on a bicycle in 1956 were a cheerful example of it.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1940s–50s; first for bicycle riding) for calf-length casual women’s trousers — a practical summer fashion, judged by Scripture’s abiding rule to adorn themselves in modest apparel (1Ti 2:9).
webster_full: PEDAL PUSHERS, n. pl. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s) Calf-length casual trousers for women and girls, originally designed for bicycle riding. "She wore her pedal pushers and saddle shoes to the church picnic."
Decode for families: what Grandma called pedal pushers you might call capris; styles change, modesty doesn’t.
scriptures: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Mat 6:29
And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
corruption_summary: A practical, wholesome garment-word with little to correct; it simply raises the abiding question of modesty that every generation’s fashion must answer.
corruption_paragraphs: Pedal pushers names a sensible garment for a bicycle and a summer day, and there is no sin in the word. The arguments families once had over them are a reminder that every age wrestles with what is fitting, and good-hearted Christians did not always agree.

The abiding rule is not a hemline but a heart: modest apparel, shamefacedness, and sobriety (1Ti 2:9), with the inward ornament prized above the outward (1Pe 3:4). A family that teaches the principle will be ready for each new fashion; a family that teaches only a list will be out of date in ten years.
roots_summary: Latin pes, pedis (foot) → pedal (foot lever) + pusher → pedal pushers (1940s), cyclists’ trousers → 1950s casual summer wear.
roots_lines: Latin pes, pedis — foot; pedal, a lever worked by the foot
Latin pulsare via French pousser — to push
1940s: pedal pushers, calf-length trousers for bicycle riding
1950s: a casual summer staple; later called capris
usage: "Your grandmother rode her bicycle to the library every Saturday in her pedal pushers, with her books in the basket."
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel (1Ti 2:9).
Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow (Mat 6:28).

etymology: American fashion word of the 1950s for a wide, full-circle felt skirt decorated with an appliqué poodle, often with a rhinestone collar and a looping leash. The felt circle skirt is commonly traced to California fashion of the late 1940s; the poodle became its most famous decoration, and by the mid-1950s the skirt, worn over petticoats with bobby socks and saddle shoes, was the very picture of the teenage girl at a sock hop.
biblical_def: For a girl in 1955, nothing said party like a poodle skirt: a great circle of pink or gray felt that swirled out when she spun on the dance floor, a little felt poodle stitched near the hem, and two or three crinoline petticoats underneath to make it stand out. Mothers sewed them at the kitchen table; girls added their own touches. It was a cheerful, girlish fashion, and on the whole a modest one, falling well below the knee. Scripture has room for that kind of delight. The prophet compares the joy of salvation to dressing up: "as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels" (Isa 61:10). Yet the same Scripture keeps clothing in its place. Women are to "adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9), and the truest ornament is "the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:4). Proverbs adds a word every teenage girl needs: "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30). And Isaiah’s verse holds the best news of all: "he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness" (Isa 61:10). A grandmother who still has her poodle skirt in a cedar chest can show it to her granddaughter and tell her both stories: how much fun it was to twirl, and how much better it is to be clothed by Christ.
webster_summary: Silent Generation fashion word (American, 1950s) for the full felt circle skirt with an appliquéd poodle, worn over petticoats at the sock hop — cheerful and modest, and a picture of the robe of righteousness (Isa 61:10).
webster_full: POODLE SKIRT, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) A wide, full-circle felt skirt decorated with an appliqué poodle, usually worn over crinoline petticoats. "Mom stayed up till midnight sewing the poodle on my skirt for the dance."
Webster (1828) — SKIRT, noun 1. The lower and loose part of a coat or other garment; the part below the waist; as the skirt of a coat or mantle. 4. A woman’s garment like a petticoat.
Decode for families: a twirl in a felt skirt was innocent fun; the lasting garment is the robe of righteousness.
scriptures: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
corruption_summary: A cheerful, generally modest fashion with nothing to correct in itself; the only caution is the old one against making clothing the measure of a girl’s worth.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no sin in a poodle skirt. It was a homemade, girlish fashion, usually sewn by mothers and worn to chaperoned dances, and by any standard it was modest. Delight in pretty clothes is not vanity in itself; Scripture uses a bride’s adornment as a picture of salvation (Isa 61:10).

The caution is about where a girl’s heart rests. A teenage world that ranks girls by the newest skirt teaches them to seek favour, which is deceitful (Pro 31:30). A Christian family can enjoy the old fashion and still teach that the hidden ornament of a meek and quiet spirit is what God calls of great price (1Pe 3:4).
roots_summary: German Pudelhund (splash-dog, a water retriever) → English poodle + Old Norse skyrta (shirt) → English skirt → poodle skirt (1950s).
roots_lines: German Pudelhund — a water dog, from Low German pudeln, to splash
Old Norse skyrta — shirt, tunic; English skirt, the lower garment
Late 1940s: the felt circle skirt in California fashion
1950s: the appliqué poodle; petticoats, bobby socks, saddle shoes
usage: "I still have my pink poodle skirt in the cedar chest. It swirled out like a parasol when I spun."
I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God (Isa 61:10).
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain (Pro 31:30).

etymology: American slang of the early 1940s for a teenage girl, from the bobby socks (short white ankle socks) worn with saddle shoes. The word became famous with the screaming young fans of the singer Frank Sinatra during his New York Paramount Theatre appearances of 1942–44, and the 1947 film The Bachelor and the Bobby-Soxer fixed it in the national vocabulary. A bobby-soxer was any devoted teenage girl fan, swooning over a crooner or a film star.
biblical_def: In 1944 the bobby-soxers lined up around the block at the Paramount Theatre in New York, thousands of teenage girls in white ankle socks and saddle shoes, waiting through the night to scream and swoon for a skinny young crooner. Some of them were your great-grandmothers. Most outgrew it, married, raised families, and laughed about it later. But the bobby-soxer was the first great picture of something our age now takes for granted: young people pouring their adoration onto a celebrity. Scripture calls that kind of devotion by its old name. "Thou shalt have no other gods before me" (Exo 20:3), and the apostle’s last word in his letter is tender and blunt: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1Jn 5:21). Stars are only men and women. When the crowd at Lystra tried to worship Paul and Barnabas, they rent their clothes and cried, "We also are men of like passions with you" (Act 14:15). "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help" (Psa 146:3) — nor in crooners either. The longing behind the swoon is real; young hearts were made to adore. Only One is worthy of it. Christ is the Beloved who never disappoints, and a heart that has learned to worship Him can enjoy a good song without giving the singer what belongs to God.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, early 1940s; the Sinatra fans of the Paramount years) for a teenage girl devotee in bobby socks and saddle shoes — the first picture of celebrity adoration, met by Scripture’s word: keep yourselves from idols (1Jn 5:21).
webster_full: BOBBY-SOXER, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s) A teenage girl, especially an ardent fan of a popular singer or film star; from the short white bobby socks then in fashion. "The bobby-soxers were lined up around the block by six in the morning."
Decode for families: every generation has its idols; the old word helps us see our own.
scriptures: Exo 20:3
Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
corruption_summary: A mostly affectionate word for teenage girls, but it names the beginning of modern celebrity worship, which Scripture calls idolatry.
corruption_paragraphs: Most bobby-soxers were simply girls having fun, and their screaming was more enthusiasm than worship. Nobody needs to be ashamed of a teenage crush on a singer, and the grandmothers who tell the story with a laugh are right to laugh.

Still, the bobby-soxer marked something new: a whole generation of young people trained by radio, records, and film to adore people they had never met. That training grew into the celebrity worship of later decades. Scripture’s warning is simple and loving: keep yourselves from idols (1Jn 5:21), and put not your trust in princes (Psa 146:3).
roots_summary: bob (cut short) + socks → bobby socks, short ankle socks (1940s) → bobby-soxer, teenage girl (early 1940s) → the Sinatra fan → any adoring teenage fan.
roots_lines: bob — to cut short (compare bobbed hair)
Early 1940s: bobby socks, short white ankle socks worn with saddle shoes
1942–44: the Sinatra crowds at the New York Paramount
1947: The Bachelor and the Bobby-Soxer fixes the word nationally
Later: any adoring teenage fan
usage: "I was a bobby-soxer in ’44. I screamed so loud at the Paramount I couldn’t talk for two days."
Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1Jn 5:21).
Thou shalt have no other gods before me (Exo 20:3).

etymology: American courtship term. Steady for a regular sweetheart is recorded early in the twentieth century; the phrase going steady was the standard teenage term of the 1940s and 1950s for an exclusive dating relationship, often marked by a class ring worn on a chain or wrapped in yarn, or a letter jacket. In the postwar years it became the usual pattern of high-school romance, and it was understood as a step short of engagement.
biblical_def: In 1955, when a boy asked a girl to go steady, he gave her his class ring, and she wore it on a chain around her neck or wrapped the band in angora yarn so it would fit her finger. Everyone at school knew what it meant: they were a couple, and nobody else need ask her to the dance. Some of those couples married and are celebrating sixty years; many broke up by spring. Scripture has a great deal to say about this road, because it is the road to marriage. Marriage is a good goal: "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD" (Pro 18:22), and "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled" (Heb 13:4). The one to go steady with must share the faith: "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers" (2Co 6:14). And the long months of an exclusive teenage romance carry their own danger, which the Song warns of three times: "that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). Paul gives the standard for the whole season: "That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour" (1Th 4:4). Going steady at fourteen with no thought of marriage often stirred up love long before it could please. A grandparent can bless the ring on the chain and still counsel patience, purity, and prayer, pointing to Christ, the Bridegroom who keeps His promises.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1940s–50s) for an exclusive teenage romance, marked by a class ring on a chain — a step on the road toward marriage, under the Song’s charge to stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please (Son 2:7).
webster_full: GOING STEADY, v. phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s) Dating one person exclusively, often signified by wearing the other’s class ring or jacket; a stage short of engagement. "Jimmy gave me his class ring — we’re going steady!"
Decode for families: going steady was meant to lead somewhere; dating with no thought of marriage often led to heartbreak.
scriptures: Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD.
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
Son 2:7
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;
corruption_summary: An honest courtship word, but the custom of long exclusive romances among young teenagers, far from marriage, often stirred up love before its time.
corruption_paragraphs: Going steady named something better than casual dating: loyalty to one person, publicly declared. Many lifelong marriages began with a class ring on a chain, and the word deserves a kind hearing.

The trouble lay in the age and the aim. Fourteen-year-olds going steady for a year with no prospect of marriage were pressed toward a closeness they were not ready to keep pure, and the breakups taught them to give their hearts away and take them back again. Scripture’s counsel is to wait for love’s proper time (Son 2:7), to choose a believer (2Co 6:14), and to walk the road to marriage in sanctification and honour (1Th 4:4).
roots_summary: Old English stede (place), stedig (firm) → English steady → early 20th c. steady, a regular sweetheart → 1940s–50s going steady, exclusive teenage dating.
roots_lines: Old English stede — place; stedig, firm, stable
English steady — firm, constant, not wavering
Early 20th c.: steady, a regular sweetheart
1940s–50s: going steady; the class ring on a chain
Understood as a step short of pinned and engaged
usage: "We went steady my whole senior year, and I wore his class ring on a chain until he traded it for a wedding band."
Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing (Pro 18:22).
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled (Heb 13:4).

etymology: American college slang of the 1940s and 1950s: a girl was pinned when her boyfriend gave her his fraternity pin to wear, a public promise more serious than going steady and understood as a step toward engagement. The custom belonged to campuses with Greek-letter fraternities and was widely recognized across the country in the postwar decades.
biblical_def: On a college campus in 1957, a girl who came back to the dormitory wearing her boyfriend’s fraternity pin over her heart was pinned, and her friends would gather around to see it. It was more than going steady and less than engaged: a public promise that they intended to marry. Sometimes the fraternity brothers serenaded her under her window. The custom has faded, but it pictures something Scripture loves: a visible token of a promise. The bride of the Song says, "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death" (Son 8:6). God Himself marks His people with a seal: "Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts" (2Co 1:22). In Christ, believers "were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise" (Eph 1:13), a pledge that the wedding will surely come. That is why a pin or a ring should never be given lightly. Our Lord taught plain dealing in every promise: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). A young man who pins a girl and then drifts away has broken a promise, however small the token. A grandparent can tell the old story with a smile and add the lesson: keep your word in love, as Christ keeps His word to His bride, the church, and never takes back His seal.
webster_summary: Silent Generation college slang (American, 1940s–50s) for a girl wearing her boyfriend’s fraternity pin, a public promise short of engagement — a token like the seal of the Song: set me as a seal upon thine heart (Son 8:6).
webster_full: PINNED, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; college) Wearing a boyfriend’s fraternity pin as a sign of a serious understanding, short of formal engagement. "Did you hear? Betty got pinned last night, and the whole house came out to sing."
Webster (1828) — PIN, noun [Latin penna, pinna.] 1. A small pointed instrument made of brass wire and headed; used chiefly by females for fastening their clothes.
Decode for families: the pin was a promise you could see; a promise should never be given lightly.
scriptures: Son 8:6
Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.
Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts.
Eph 1:13
In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
corruption_summary: A sweet courtship word with nothing wrong in it; the only caution is that a visible promise given lightly, and broken easily, teaches the young to make vows cheaply.
corruption_paragraphs: Pinned names a custom of honest, public intention, and there is nothing to correct in the word. A young man declaring before his friends that he means to marry a girl is doing something good.

The caution is in the breaking. Pins were sometimes given in the excitement of a party and taken back by spring, and each broken token taught that promises are provisional. Scripture asks that our yea be yea (Mat 5:37), and the God who seals His people with His Spirit (Eph 1:13) never takes the seal back.
roots_summary: Old English pinn (peg; perhaps from Latin pinna, point) → English pin → the fraternity pin → 1940s–50s pinned, promised short of engagement.
roots_lines: Old English pinn — a peg or bolt; perhaps from Latin pinna, a point
English pin — a fastening; a badge or brooch
19th–20th c.: the fraternity pin, worn by members
1940s–50s: pinned, wearing his pin as a pledge short of engagement
The ladder: going steady, pinned, engaged, married
usage: "Your grandmother was pinned for six months before I could afford a ring."
Set me as a seal upon thine heart (Son 8:6).
Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts (2Co 1:22).

etymology: American English. Teens for the years of life ending in -teen is centuries old; the adjective teen-age is recorded from the early twentieth century, and the noun teen-ager appears in American print by the early 1940s. During and after the war, advertisers and magazines took up the word for a newly distinct group of young people with their own money, music, and clothes, and by the 1950s the teenager was a fixed figure in American life. The Silent Generation were the first to grow up under the name.
biblical_def: Grandpa’s own father was never a teenager; he was a boy, and then a young man with a job and responsibilities. The word itself came into its own in the 1940s, when advertisers and magazines began to speak of a separate age between childhood and adulthood, with its own records, clothes, slang, and spending money. The Silent Generation were the first to be called by the name. Scripture does not use the word, but it knows the season well and speaks to it with great dignity. "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity" (1Ti 4:12). Timothy was not told to wait for adulthood to be faithful. The great call to the young is "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth" (Ecc 12:1). And the young are to grow up, not stay young: "when I became a man, I put away childish things" (1Co 13:11). Most precious of all, our Lord Himself passed through these years. Of the boy Jesus it is written: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man" (Luk 2:52). There is no teenager whose years Christ did not sanctify by living them. A grandparent can tell a grandchild that the teen years are not a holiday from responsibility but a training ground, and that the Lord who was once a young man walks with the young.
webster_summary: Silent Generation coinage (American, early 1940s; from the old word teens) for a young person aged thirteen to nineteen as a distinct group — a season Scripture dignifies: let no man despise thy youth (1Ti 4:12).
webster_full: TEENAGER, n. (Silent Generation coinage, 1940s; at first spelled teen-ager) A person between thirteen and nineteen years of age, especially as a member of a distinct social and commercial group. "The magazine says teenagers spent a fortune on records last year."
Webster (1828) — TEENS, noun [from teen, ten.] The years of one’s age reckoned by the termination teen. These years begin with thirteen, and end with nineteen.
Decode for families: the Silent Generation were the first teenagers; the Bible calls the season youth and gives it a calling.
scriptures: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Ecc 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
Luk 2:52
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
corruption_summary: A neutral word, but it came with an idea — youth as a separate world with its own rules and market — that can excuse the young from the responsibility Scripture expects of them.
corruption_paragraphs: Teenager is a useful, harmless word, and nobody needs to stop saying it. The years from thirteen to nineteen are real and distinct, and Scripture speaks often to the young (Ecc 12:1; 1Ti 4:12).

What came with the word deserves a second look. The teenager was shaped partly as a market, and markets profit when the young are kept young: separated from adults, absorbed in their own music and fashions, and excused from serious duty. Scripture expects more. It calls the young to be examples to the believers (1Ti 4:12), to flee youthful lusts (2Ti 2:22), and to put away childish things (1Co 13:11), following the Lord who increased in wisdom and stature (Luk 2:52).
roots_summary: Old English tien (ten) → -teen (thirteen to nineteen) → teens (years of youth) → teen-age (early 20th c.) → teen-ager (early 1940s) → teenager.
roots_lines: Old English tien, tyn — ten; the suffix -teen
teens — the years thirteen through nineteen
Early 20th c.: teen-age, adjective
Early 1940s: teen-ager, noun, in American print
1950s: teenager, a fixed figure in American life and advertising
usage: "When I was your age nobody called us teenagers. We were just old enough to work."
Let no man despise thy youth (1Ti 4:12).
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth (Ecc 12:1).
